record.paper_title: Solving the Integrated Bin Allocation and Collection Routing Problem for Municipal Solid Waste: a Benders Decomposition Approach
record.context_brief: Scalability on larger real-world MSW instances
record.original_question: For a garbage-accumulation-point municipal solid waste system, where residents deposit waste at shared garbage accumulation points and planners must jointly choose the locations and capacities of waste-bin combinations together with collection vehicle routes and schedules, can the Benders-decomposition-based mixed-integer programming approach for this integrated bin-allocation and collection-routing problem be tested on larger real-world instances than the Bahía Blanca instances evaluated so far, and what computational performance does it achieve on those larger instances?

evidence.quote: When using GAPs, MSW management comprises the following design decisions: – The design of a pre-collection network, which consists in defining the location and capacity of GAPs. – The design and schedule of routes for collection vehicles.
We performed computational experiments using our approach on a set of real-world instances of two important neighbourhoods of the Argentinean city of Bahía Blanca.
Future work includes expanding computational experiments with larger real-world instances to test the scalability of the approach.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a municipal solid waste (MSW) management system organized around Garbage Accumulation Points (GAPs): designated shared locations where residents deposit waste, each of which can be equipped with a combination of bins of various capacities chosen from a finite catalogue. Given:

- a set of candidate GAP locations together with the demand (waste generation rate) of the residential blocks assigned to each location,
- a catalogue of bin types with associated capacities and costs,
- a fleet of homogeneous collection vehicles with finite capacity operating out of a depot, and
- a planning horizon partitioned into periods (e.g., days of the week) with collection-frequency requirements,

the integrated bin-allocation and collection-routing problem is to jointly decide (i) the location of GAPs and the combination of bins installed at each opened GAP, and (ii) the periodic routes and schedules of collection vehicles, so as to minimize the total installation and routing cost while satisfying capacity, demand, frequency, and routing constraints. Formulate this as a mixed-integer program and design a Benders-decomposition-based exact algorithm that separates the bin-allocation (master) decisions from the vehicle-routing (subproblem) decisions.

Problem: Demonstrate the scalability of this Benders-decomposition approach by applying it to real-world instances substantially larger than those of two neighbourhoods of Bahía Blanca, Argentina previously considered, and characterize quantitatively the computational performance attained—optimality gaps, solution times, number of Benders iterations, and the size of instances (number of candidate GAPs, demand points, periods, and vehicles) that can be solved to proven optimality or to a prescribed gap within a given time limit.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface follow-up computational studies extending the Benders-decomposition approach for the integrated GAP bin-allocation and collection-routing problem to real-world MSW instances larger than the Bahía Blanca neighbourhoods. The scalability question therefore appears to remain open in the published literature, but absence of evidence is not conclusive.

status_evidence.title: Solving the Integrated Bin Allocation and Collection Routing Problem for Municipal Solid Waste
status_evidence.snippet: Future work includes expanding computational experiments with larger real-world instances to test the scalability of the approach.
status_evidence.claim: The original work explicitly leaves larger-scale computational testing as future work, and no later study extending the experiments has been located.
